mainEntity.name: Are short dental implants as reliable as standard-length implants?

acceptedAnswer.text: Clinical research suggests that modern short dental implants, when correctly indicated and placed using appropriate techniques, may achieve long-term success rates comparable to standard-length implants in appropriately selected cases, though individual outcomes will vary. Improvements in implant surface design have significantly improved osseointegration outcomes. However, success depends on careful patient selection and thorough pre-treatment assessment. Not all patients with limited bone height will be suitable for short implants, and your clinician will discuss the most appropriate option for your individual anatomy.

mainEntity.name: How do I know if I need a sinus lift or if short implants are an option for me?

acceptedAnswer.text: This can only be determined through a clinical assessment that includes detailed radiographic imaging, typically a cone beam CT scan. The decision depends on the exact amount and quality of bone available, the proximity of the sinus floor, and other anatomical and medical factors. There is no reliable way to assess this from a photograph or from a standard dental X-ray alone. A consultation with an experienced implant clinician is the appropriate next step.

mainEntity.name: How long does treatment with short dental implants take compared to having a sinus lift?

acceptedAnswer.text: If short implants are clinically suitable, they may allow treatment to be completed more efficiently because the augmentation and healing stages associated with a sinus lift are not required. However, the implants still require a period of osseointegration before the final crown is attached, typically around three to six months. Exact timelines will depend on individual healing, bone quality, and the treatment protocol used by your clinician.

mainEntity.name: Is the placement of short dental implants painful?

acceptedAnswer.text: Dental implant placement, including short implants, is typically performed under local anaesthesia. Many patients report feeling pressure during the procedure rather than pain, though individual experience varies. Post-operative discomfort is generally manageable with over-the-counter pain relief and usually settles within a few days. Your dental team will provide detailed aftercare guidance and will advise you on what to expect following your specific procedure.

mainEntity.name: Can short dental implants be used in the lower jaw as well?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, short dental implants may also be considered in the lower jaw, particularly in areas where the inferior alveolar nerve limits available bone height. The principles of assessment are similar — bone height, width, and density are evaluated through imaging to determine suitability. Your clinician will assess both arches as part of a comprehensive treatment planning process if implants are being considered in multiple areas.

mainEntity.name: What happens if short implants are not suitable for me?

acceptedAnswer.text: If short implants are not appropriate for your individual anatomy, your clinician will explain the reasons clearly and discuss alternative options. These may include sinus augmentation combined with standard implants, bone grafting procedures, implant-supported bridges, or implant-retained dentures, depending on your specific situation. The aim is always to find a clinically sound solution that meets your needs and expectations in a realistic and honest way.
